titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Ecuador

div.head: 369. Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Ecuador
div.p: 2. Summary: Ambassador Enders met with President Roldos for one hour and 45 minutes in Houston on April 12. The atmosphere was very cordial and constructive. Principal topics of discussion were the situations in Central America, the future of human rights and democracy in the hemisphere, the Peru/Ecuador border dispute, U.S. arms sales policy and the tuna issue. We believe the meeting was quite useful. End summary.

3. Ecuadorean President Jaime Roldos accompanied by Ambassador to the U.S. Crespo and OAS Ambassador Falconi received Ambassador Enders and ARA/AND Director Hart for one hour and 45 minutes conversation in Houston on April 12. The atmospherics of the talks were completely relaxed and positive. The main points which emerged are summarized below.

4. The future of democracy. Roldos opened by observing that there is no single Latin American view on what the proper U.S. or Latin American policy should be
toward the promotion of democracy. Many Latin Americans have a superficial and emotional perception that the U.S. is allied with the “haves” in the hemisphere. They resent what they believe is overemphasis of the communist danger. Roldos does not think that Latin America and U.S. goals are contradictory. We both want democracy and reject the idea that anti-communism means denial of social justice. We share the concern about the efforts of the small but well-organized extremists of the right and left in Latin America to capture the initiative from the much more numerous (maybe 90 percent of the population) moderate forces. The extremes use any tactics to polarize societies rather than to work for gradual social, economic and political progress. Again, there is no difference with the U.S. on this approach. At the same time, there may be a wave of “new mercantilism” developing in the region to the detriment of democracy. The military play a powerful role in all the Latin American countries, including those with civilian constitutional governments. Because of the international economic crisis which all but the large oil exporting countries must face, governments are forced to concentrate on financial problems such as inflation and the balance of payments. Social programs to a large extent have had to be deferred despite the widening gap in the economic/social structure which had occurred as the result of economic growth in 1960’s and 1970’s. This plays into the hands of the communists and others who adopt pseudo-popularist rhetoric to fool the public. Where communism has been clearly posed as an alternative to the people, it has been rejected. Everyone knows that the experiment in Cuba has failed. In response to Ambassador Enders’ observation that there were also positive developments concerning democracy, and Roldos commented that Mexico, Venezuela and Brazil were the most important countries in the region for the U.S. and probably will serve Latin America as different models for democracy building.

5. Human rights. Enders outlined our new approach to human rights, using private rather than public diplomacy. Roldos did not respond directly, but talked about the need to lower the emotional content of the political debate within countries and to avoid the polarization that the extremists seek. Human rights in Latin America is linked mentally with the constitutional process. Protection of human rights is not a position of weakness; it’s a policy of strength on which we cannot turn our backs. Respect for human rights is needed to give credit to the center and
discredit the extremes. In this respect, Roldos placed particular value on the direct dialogue he has established with Viola in Argentina. He mentioned that he may visit Brazil in October and is considering plans to meet soon with Herrera of Venezuela and Royo of Panama.

6. Central America. After Enders’ observation that it is precisely the need to strengthen the center which is at the heart of the problem in El Salvador and elsewhere in Central America, Roldos offered the opinion that many in Latin America see Duarte as being too closely tied to the junta. Duarte has a creditability problem because people see the Salvadoran political situation in black and white. Roldos mentioned his meeting with Duarte in Santa Marta.

7. The border conflict. Roldos thanked the U.S. warmly for its help in the recent crises. In his view, there has been a change in Ecuador’s attitude on the settlement of this problem. Although there is no national consensus on the shape of the solution and the emotional content on the subject is very high, Ecuador has now lowered its sights on what can be achieved. It wants a friendly solution. Unfortunately, Peru has been very hard-nosed and has been unwilling to discuss even the more modest ideas Ecuador has put forward. On a strictly private basis, Enders suggested that a look at some of the European arrangements for river use might provide imaginative ideas which would give Ecuador an outlet to the Amazon.

8. Arms purchase by Ecuador. Roldos was told that the U.S. understood Ecuador’s feelings that it had to buy new aircraft at this time. Under our new arms policy, we had approved the sales of the Kfir and F–5. At the same time, we believe it’s important that direct and frank dialogue be establish with Peru on delicate matters such as this to avoid a misinterpretation of motives. Given Peru’s deep suspicion of Ecuador’s intentions, Peru probably would respond with large arms purchases of its own to the announcement of an Ecuadorean buy. Roldos replied that it is ridiculous to believe that Ecuador is a military threat to Peru. The planes would be purely for defense. Ecuador needs some kind of deterrent capability against Peru’s overwhelming military superiority. Roldos left the impression that Ecuador would buy the Kfirs fairly soon. He did not react to the suggestion that communication with Peru on this and other subjects by someone like Galo Plaza is desirable.

9. Tuna. There was an agreement that both sides want to avoid having the tuna boat seizure problem interfere with our excellent overall relations. We must search for practical solutions to avoid conflicts which could arise because of our different political
and juridical position. Enders explained how we might soon be faced with a difficult situation in the Congress when a replenishment of funds for the Fisherman’s Protective Act is considered. There will be congressmen who will want to deduct payments to U.S. tuna boats seized by Ecuador from our foreign assistance. If the present situation continues it will be hard to say they are wrong. We want to continue aid to Ecuador and believe it would be very useful if we can begin soon to discuss an interim solution to our dispute pending the outcome of law of the sea negotiations. Enders mentioned the Micronesia Tuna Agreement as worth consideration as a way of having a modus vivendi while leaving our juridical positions intact. Negotiations between the U.S. and Ecuadorean Fishing Association might be the best way to look at the problem. They might find some contractual basis on which they want to do business. Roldos said he wanted to avoid a vicious circle of conflict over tuna. He had no problem with discussions between the US and Ecuadorean fishery industries. It was agreed that further talks between ourselves and Ecuador on how we wish to proceed should take place. Ambassador Crespo and Hart will be in touch.

Comment: Our main objective in this meeting was to establish a constructive personal relationship between Ambassador Enders and the President. We also wished to probe Roldos’ views on hemispheric problems and to provide our own thoughts on selective regional and bilateral matters. We are satisfied that both goals were accomplished.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810177–0671. Confidential; Immediate; Exdis. Sent for information Priority to Lima, Caracas, Mexico City, Brasilia, Buenos Aires, San Salvador, Bogota, USSOUTHCOM, and CINCLANT. Drafted by Hart; cleared in S/S–O and ARA; approved by Enders.
See Document 368 and footnotes 2 and 3 thereto.

In telegram 43870 to Quito and Lima, February 20, the Department wrote about the sale of Israeli Kfirs to Ecuador: “Department informed Israelis on February 20 that we are favorably disposed toward to the sale and intends to notify Congress of intent to approve sale as soon as Peru-Ecuador situation permits. We briefed them on reasons for delay. We will seek GOI assurances that they will consult with the USG on the delivery schedule for the Kfirs (assuming sale is consummated) in order that the timing of their arrival does not come at a critical stage in the negotiations or a period of high tension between Ecuador and Peru.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810080–0879)

In telegram 43798 to Quito and Lima, February 20, the Department wrote: “We believe it is necessary to discuss frankly with the Governments in Quito and Lima the policy we are applying to their arms requests so long as the serious threat of hostilities between those countries persists. Therefore, the following talking points are provided for Ambassadors Corr and Gonzalez to use promptly at the highest level of their host governments: —Since the outbreak of hostilities, we have received requests from both countries for various kinds of military equipment and supplies (FYI principally from Ecuador). —We have been processing these requests in a routine manner. —Our policy of normal processing includes the application of the same criteria for case-by-case decisions to both countries and is intended to avoid any indication of favoritism. —We would like to impress on both governments how important we believe it is that they not increase military expenditures as a result of the unfortunate border incident. —Unusually difficult decisions are required when major items of hardware, such as combat aircraft, are involved. As you know, we have authorized in principle the sale of F–5E/F’s, A–37’s and T–37’s to Ecuador and Peru and conveyed an initially favorable response to the Israeli’s on sale of Kfirs to Ecuador. You should be aware, however, and you may so inform Peru and Ecuador, that we will take a close look at the prospect of conflict between the two countries before delivery of any major weapon system is actually carried out.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810082–0423)

A June 5 Department of State paper noted: “Ecuador signed an agreement with Israel in late May to purchase 12 Kfir fighters and is continuing negotiations for six more. Six Kfirs were being moved out of a storage area in the last week of May for probable sea delivery to Ecuador, according to the Defense Attaché in Tel Aviv. INR Comment: Ecuador probably chose the Kfirs because they can shipped more rapidly than US-built F–5’s; Ecuador’s military reportedly fears renewed conflict with Peru later this year. The deal is Israel’s first export of the Kfir. Latin America accounted for just over one-half of Israel’s total arms deliveries between 1976 and 1980.” (Reagan Library, Roger W. Fontaine Files, Subject File, Ecuador [January 1981–June 1981])

In telegram 82 from Guayaquil, January 16, the Consulate reported: “U.S. flag tuna boat Rosa D was seized by an Ecuadorian naval vessel January 15, 1981.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810023–0565) In telegram 20466 to Quito, January 27, the Department transmitted talking points for Gonzalez to use in a démarche to Roldós, indicating that “the USG is seriously concerned over the seizure of the Rosa D and the January 19 decision of the San Cristobal tribunal to penalize the Rosa D under Ecuadorean law as if it had been illegally fishing.” The evidence suggested that “the Rosa D was simply transiting the waters off the coast of Ecuador,” the talking points noted, “and a GOE decision to fine the boat and confiscate the fish on board the Rosa D would be viewed with great seriousness.” The Department also instructed Gonzalez to “mention to Roldos that in wake of this recent seizure and hopeful that a resolution can be worked out, it is perhaps a propitious time for USG and GOE representatives to meet to consider a solution to this problem. The USG is ready to engage in exploratory technical talks.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810038–1165)
